details:
**Middlemarch**
Eliot's most famous novel (1871–72), subtitled "A Study of Provincial Life" and set in a fictional Midlands town around 1830. Its idealistic heroine is Dorothea Brooke. It ends by praising those who "lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs." Early on, Dorothea and her sister Celia divide their dead mother's jewels, and Dorothea takes only an emerald ring and bracelet.

**Edward Casaubon and The Key to All Mythologies**
Casaubon is the dry, aging clergyman-scholar whom Dorothea marries, hoping to help with his great work. He never finishes The Key to All Mythologies, an outdated attempt to trace all myths to a single source, and he rejects her help. Before he dies, he adds a clause to his will that takes away her inheritance if she marries his young cousin Will Ladislaw. She gives up the fortune and marries Will anyway.

**Tertius Lydgate and Rosamond Vincy**
Lydgate is an ambitious young doctor in Middlemarch whose career is ruined by debt and by his marriage to the pretty, selfish Rosamond Vincy. The kind vicar Camden Farebrother is among those who try to help him.

**Nicholas Bulstrode and John Raffles**
Bulstrode is Middlemarch's hypocritical, Evangelical banker who lends money to Lydgate. The drunken John Raffles blackmails him over his past: Bulstrode made his fortune in a pawnbroking business that dealt in stolen goods, and he hid the fact that the rightful heir to that money (Will Ladislaw's mother) was alive. When Raffles dies in Bulstrode's care, the resulting scandal also stains Lydgate. Another subplot involves the miser Peter Featherstone, who dies before he can have one of his two wills burned, so his fortune goes to his illegitimate son Joshua Rigg.

**Silas Marner**
Eliot's 1861 short novel about the "weaver of Raveloe," a lonely linen weaver. He was driven out of Lantern Yard, his religious community, after his friend William Dane framed him for theft by planting his pocketknife where a dying deacon's money had been stolen. The congregation drew lots to decide his guilt, and Dane then married Silas's fiancée Sarah.

**Dunstan Cass and Silas's gold**
Dunstan "Dunsey" Cass, the squire's wastrel son, kills his brother's horse Wildfire while out riding, then steals Silas's hoarded gold and disappears. The peddler Jem Rodney is suspected at first. Years later, Dunstan's skeleton is found in a drained stone pit, still clutching the gold.

**Eppie, Molly Farren, and Godfrey Cass**
Molly Farren, the opium-addicted secret wife of Godfrey Cass, dies in the snow on New Year's Eve on her way to the Red House to expose the marriage. Her golden-haired toddler Eppie wanders into Silas's cottage, and he adopts and raises her, finding happiness again. Godfrey marries Nancy Lammeter, and when he later claims Eppie as his daughter, she chooses to stay with Silas.

**Adam Bede**
Eliot's first novel (1859), set in the village of Hayslope and named for an upright carpenter. Adam loves the pretty, vain Hetty Sorrel, who is seduced by the young squire Arthur Donnithorne. In the end Adam marries the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris, completing the book's "love rectangle."

**Hetty Sorrel's trial**
In Adam Bede, Hetty leaves town pregnant, gives birth, and abandons the baby in a field, where it dies of exposure. She is tried and sentenced to death for child murder, but Arthur arrives with a reprieve that reduces her sentence to transportation.

**The Mill on the Floss**
Eliot's 1860 novel about the siblings Tom and Maggie Tulliver of Dorlcote Mill on the river Floss. Their father loses the mill to the lawyer Wakem and writes a curse against him in the family Bible. The siblings, estranged for years, reconcile just before both drown in a flood at the end.

**Maggie Tulliver, Philip Wakem, and Stephen Guest**
Maggie is the passionate, intelligent heroine of The Mill on the Floss. As a child she lets Tom's rabbits die by forgetting to feed them, and as a teenager she turns to renunciation after reading Thomas à Kempis's The Imitation of Christ. She has a secret friendship with the hunchbacked Philip Wakem, the lawyer's son, and is disgraced after drifting downriver toward Mudport with Stephen Guest, her cousin Lucy's suitor.

**Daniel Deronda**
Eliot's last novel (1876). Daniel, raised by the wealthy Sir Hugo Mallinger, first sees Gwendolen Harleth losing at roulette and redeems the turquoise necklace she has pawned. He becomes her moral guide during her miserable marriage to Grandcourt.

**Mirah Lapidoth and Mordecai**
In Daniel Deronda, Daniel saves the Jewish singer Mirah from drowning herself in the Thames. He learns that his mother was Jewish, becomes the disciple of Mirah's visionary brother Mordecai, marries Mirah, and leaves for "the East" to work toward a Jewish homeland, a proto-Zionist ending.

**Scenes of Clerical Life**
Eliot's first fiction (1858), a collection of three stories: "The Sad Fortunes of the Reverend Amos Barton," in which Amos neglects his wife Milly for the Countess Czerlaski; "Mr. Gilfil's Love Story," in which Gilfil finds Caterina "Tina" Sarti with a knife and fears she has killed Captain Wybrow; and "Janet's Repentance."

**Mary Ann Evans, translator and critic**
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. Her first published work was a translation of David Strauss's Life of Jesus, and she also translated Feuerbach's The Essence of Christianity. She edited the Westminster Review and wrote essays such as "Silly Novels by Lady Novelists." Her other works include Felix Holt, the Radical, in which an election riot leads Felix to accidentally kill a constable as Harold Transom runs for office in Treby Magna; Romola, set in Savonarola's Florence and featuring the deceitful Tito Melema; and the verse drama The Spanish Gypsy.
